title: Sex and dating in midlife - Sharon Horgan on her new comedy Youth
description: Casual sex. Relationships. Parenting. Sharon Horgan has already seen us through several life stages via hit comedy dramas such as Pulling, Catastrophe
body: Casual sex. Relationships. Parenting. Sharon Horgan has already seen us through several life stages via hit comedy dramas such as Pulling, Catastrophe and Motherland.Now, with her latest show Youth, Horgan puts the spotlight on 50-something women, imbued with her trademark tightly balanced mix of hilarity and pathos.The HBO Max series sees Horgan's character, Alex, gamely attempting to juggle a stressful publishing career while looking after a teenage son and elderly parents. She's part of the so-called sandwich generation, those in midlife who have to juggle caring responsibilities for old and young while often working, too. And that's not all - Alex is also back in the dating game following a divorce.I'm curious to know how much of Youth is based on Horgan's own experience. The star is divorced and has two daughters."We've all got kids who are kind of adults now and parents who are getting older and ailing in some cases. There is a chunk of my life in there, an… autobiographical element for sure. But the good thing about writing autofiction is that no one really knows which bits are real and which bits aren't, I guess, except the people [in it]!"The hit writer, producer and actress mulled over the idea for Youth before going on to make Apple TV's Bad Sisters, coming back to it after the dark comedy ended.The 56-year-old says she was keen to "write about this particular time in a woman's life... through the lens of a mother of a son". Horgan wanted the story to be "post-divorce and "menopause adjacent"."And I wanted it to be a comedy, you know? Because there's a lot that's very funny about our bodies failing!"But it's not just her comedy chops that have gained her a loyal following - a big factor in Horgan's success over the last 20 years or so is the authenticity she brings to her work."I spent a lot of time trying to make it as real and as accurate as possible and trying to put in my faults as a parent and mistakes as a woman, my own sort of anxieties and insecurities," she says."I try to put all that in there… and hope that's a universal feeling because it's really madly important to me that women, especially, watch it and see themselves reflected back."She says that Youth "felt like the next stage on" from her popular sitcom Catastrophe.The series, which first aired in 2015 on Channel 4, followed the lives of 40-somethings Sharon and Rob (played by Horgan and Rob Delaney), a couple who got together suddenly after their brief transatlantic fling resulted in pregnancy."This [show] feels part of the same trajectory, almost, which was fun and really helpful when it came to trying to figure out what the tone was, although I hope it's kind of doing its own thing," Hogan explains.There are new issues to concern ourselves with in mid-life and, as you'd expect, Horgan doesn't shy away from embarrassing situations or mildly unhealthy preoccupations.Her protagonist - who is 50 - has a slight obsession with sagging skin, which will no doubt strike a chord with many."It's really weird watching yourself age on screen because that's not fun," she reveals.Horgan says she wanted to offer "an honest depiction of someone having a complicated relationship with ageing". She adds that she herself has now formed "a better relationship" with getting older."I think it's OK to age any way you want to age. And we're insecure about it for a reason. And that's because it's shoved down our necks that we need to look a certain way, especially within the entertainment industry and in magazines. And women who age really well are celebrated just for that. And that is annoying."When it comes to sex, she says "you just have different insecurities" when you're a bit older."You think about angles, you think about the shapes you make and how to be sexy as an older woman. And, you, know, lighting comes into it! But I also have friends who are incredibly free with their bodies and feel like this is a whole new era and they're embracing it."I know that I will get there," she continues. "But I wanted to show a middle-aged woman having a complicated relationship with her body but still putting herself out there because... she wants to find someone to grow old with."Sherwood star Sharlene Whyte, who plays Horgan's boss and best friend Sam, says we need to see older women's stories on screen."We should see more of it - women who are later on in age, who have been privileged to get here later on, who are still killing it and are still beautiful and sexy and funny," she says."But I think women in their 50s are more visible (now)... and there's more (acting) work for women in later life."Despite the two lead characters being 50-something women, Whyte describes Youth as "an inter-generational watch".That's probably due to a prominent Gen Z storyline involving Alex's son, Ruari, played by 19-year-old Aran Murphy (Cillian Murphy's son. And yes, as you might expect, he's very good).Ruari has a difficult relationship with his feckless father - Alex's ex-husband (Owen McDonnell) - and in one poignant scene, describes how confusing it is to find your way as a young man in today's world."Having good people around you is so important, and it's not always easy to have that," Murphy muses."So, for someone like Ruari, when you don't have the foundation of friends and stuff, you look to the (wrong) kinds of people... and oftentimes, you'll be left out on your ass with the wrong answers."What does he hope young people who might catch the show will take away from it?"You don't have to have it all in place at 18, everyone is still kind of just pretending they know what they're doing."I suggest that we don't always know what we're doing in later life either.He laughs. "Exactly. Everyone's still figuring it out."Youth will debut on 21 September in the UK & Ireland on HBO Max.

schema.headline: Sex and dating in midlife - Sharon Horgan on her new comedy Youth

title: Largest attack on Moscow sees Ukraine fire hundreds of drones, mayor says
description: Ukraine has fired its largest drone attack on the Moscow region, the mayor has said, hitting the city's main oil refinery and a residential building.M
body: Ukraine has fired its largest drone attack on the Moscow region, the mayor has said, hitting the city's main oil refinery and a residential building.Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 450 drones heading for the capital had been shot down in what he called "the most massive" attack. The region's governor said at least two people were killed and 20 injured.Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Kyiv had hit a "key" Russian oil facility and a logistics site in the region with drones and missiles, representing "billions of dollars that sustain the war machine".Ukrainian officials meanwhile said nine people, including three children, had been killed in Russian attacks in the Kyiv and Sumy regions on Saturday.Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes, targeting energy-generating and transport facilities, as well as major logistics hubs.A 44-year-old woman was killed in Sofyino on Sunday after a drone hit a three-storey residential building, regional head Andrei Vorobyev said. Another five people - including two children - were injured.An elderly man died after a private house was hit in the Orekhovo-Zuevo district, Governor Andrei Vorobyev added.Videos have emerged on social media appearing to show explosions in the night skies above Moscow, and a burning warehouse. The footage has not been verified by the BBC.Mayor Sobyanin said a drone had struck a building near one of the capital's boulevards and the oil refinery - where Ukrainian military officials said three key units had been damaged.The site supplies more than a third of the Moscow region's fuel, according to the defence ministry in Kyiv, and some of its petrol, diesel and aviation fuel go to Russia's military.Ukraine's defence minister said attacking such facilities "directly undermines the enemy's ability to continue its war of aggression and supply its military formations".Sobyanin said the major attack was "an attempt to disrupt" Russia's parliamentary election, which was in its third day on Sunday. The vote is tightly controlled by the Kremlin and has been dismissed by critics as neither free, fair nor transparent.Russian state media reported that an election official was one of two people killed by a drone attack on a bus in a Moscow-controlled part of Kherson in Ukraine on Sunday, citing the head of Russia's election commission.Meanwhile, Moscow's biggest airport Sheremetyevo warned passengers "temporary restrictions" were in place overnight, while at the capital's Vnukovo airport all arrivals and departures were halted. Restrictions at both airports were lifted by Sunday morning but each warned some flights may still be delayed.It comes after a mother and her two small children, a boy and a girl, were killed in a Russian attack in the city of Fastiv, Kyiv on Saturday, according to regional head Tymur Tkachenko.He later said a child injured in a separate attack in Vyshhorod, north of Kyiv, had also died in hospital.In the north-eastern Sumy region, four people were killed when a Russian drone hit the car they were travelling in, top local official Oleh Hryhorov said.Russia also struck a monastery in the Kherson region with a drone on Saturday, Zelensky said, killing one member of the clergy and injuring four others.Both Russia and Ukraine have continued to hit energy infrastructure targets in the past week, despite US President Donald Trump claiming on social media that the two sides had agreed not to do so.Trump signed a sanctions bill on Friday that targets Russia's economy by implementing tariffs on the biggest buyers of the country's oil and gas which include China and India.The US legislation gives the US president powers to impose 100% tariffs on major purchasers of Russian energy.Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

schema.headline: Largest attack on Moscow sees Ukraine fire hundreds of drones, mayor says

title: Why growing older LGBTQ+ community in Britain fears losing identity
description: As a 75-year-old lesbian, Mindy Meleyal has lived through every major milestone in the modern LGBT rights movement, from the start of decriminalisatio
body: As a 75-year-old lesbian, Mindy Meleyal has lived through every major milestone in the modern LGBT rights movement, from the start of decriminalisation in 1967 to the first same-sex marriages in 2014.But now she says this important part of her identity is frequently overlooked due to her age.She's part of England's older LGBTQ+ community, which a new report suggests often experiences poorer health, more limited finances and greater social isolation than the wider older population.The report, from the Centre for Ageing Better, says without specialist support, this growing demographic could be forced "back into the closet" when accessing care, warning they may even delay getting the care they need because of concerns about homophobia.Adam Porter, a housing development manager from the LGBT Foundation charity, says he regularly meets older members of the community in exactly that situation."It's very common for people to hide things if they have a carer visiting their home, for example hiding their wedding photos or taking down a trans flag," he says."In the case of someone moving into a care environment, that means hiding who they are in their own home, for what could be the rest of their life."He says he has been "horrified" by some of the stories he has heard meeting older LGBTQ+ people, including some who have had carers offer to "pray for them" regarding their sexuality.Porter is part of the team behind Kindred House, a first-of-its-kind LGBTQ+ social housing scheme for over-55s, set to open in Manchester next year.But despite having their support while he's relatively independent, Norman says he worries about the prospect of facing discrimination if he needs more formal care as he ages."Hopefully I will maintain and look after myself the best I can, but I've heard horror stories of gay people in nursing homes being treated terribly," he says."I think nurses, doctors, carers should all be trained on how to look after LGBT people."It's the reason behind schemes like Manchester's Kindred House, which are not unusual in other parts of the world.There are similar projects in Spain, Sweden, Germany, the US and Canada, but in the UK they are few and far between.In 2021, the UK's first LGBTQ+ retirement home, Tonic, opened in London with 19 apartments for private rental or shared ownership.The scheme attracted so much attention, later this year it is set to feature in a Netflix documentary telling the story of one of its first residents, Chek Min-Ong.After 43 years together, Min, 77, and his late partner Tim, had discussed their plans for a future where one of them would live alone, as Tim's health deteriorated.While schemes like Kindred House and Tonic are welcomed by Mindy, Norman and Min, the Spotlight on Ageing report warns that, because the older LGBTQ+ population is growing, the demand for specialist services is expected to outstrip supply.Between 2019 and 2024, the number of over-50s identifying as lesbian, gay or bisexual in the UK increased by around a third - from roughly 340,000 to almost 460,000.There was a 4% rise in the number of heterosexual people aged 50 and above in the same period.These numbers are projected to continue to increase as the relatively larger younger generations of people identifying as LGBTQ+ age.Porter warns that without more schemes like Kindred House, and more training and awareness for those in other care settings, the ageing population may struggle to get proper support.For Mindy, who is part of a steering group advising on the plans, knowing there may be more options available in the future is reassuring."It's important that you can go, that you think, 'You know what, I could live there because I know the staffing, the ethics, the rules, everything about the place has been put together from an LGBTQ+ focus,'" she says."That's what we've been doing and it's something I'm really proud of being a part of."

schema.headline: Why growing older LGBTQ+ community in Britain fears losing identity

title: The deadly new drugs making Scotland's fight against addiction even harder
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Nitazenes are a class of synthetic opioids often sold as heroinByScotland editorUpdated 7 hours agoEfforts to
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Nitazenes are a class of synthetic opioids often sold as heroinByScotland editorUpdated 7 hours agoEfforts to bring down Scotland's sky-high rate of drug deaths are being frustrated by the arrival of hundreds of powerful new synthetic substances that experts warn are making the deadly drugs crisis even more dangerous.  In the past three years, there has been an explosion in the supply of new synthetic cannabinoids and opioids, transforming the illicit drugs trade and increasing the risk of fatal overdoses.Annual figures to be released on Wednesday are expected to show a rise in the number of drug-related deaths in Scotland, which already has an unenviable record as the drugs death capital of Europe."The illicit drug supply in Scotland is getting more and more dangerous," said Dr Lorna Nisbet of Dundee University's Leverhulme Research Centre for Forensic Science.Image caption, Forensic scientist Lorna Nisbet says the illicit drug supply in Scotland is getting more dangerousUnlike heroin or cocaine, which are derived from cultivated plants, many of the new substances are manufactured in clandestine laboratories. They include synthetic opioids such as nitazenes and orphines, some of which are hundreds of times more potent than heroin.Police say organised crime groups are increasingly mixing the substances with existing drugs to maximise their profits."I think it's shameful behaviour that we're seeing from these organised crime groups," Supt Niven Bull, of Police Scotland, said."They are profiting from people's misery."On average, a new psychoactive substance emerged every week in 2025, according to the European Union Drugs Agency (EUDA)., external The agency says tighter controls imposed by China and the Taliban's ban on poppy cultivation in Afghanistan have pushed production closer to consumer markets.That includes Scotland, where police have raided two suspected nitazene factories in the past 14 months, making five arrests in total.In July 2025, officers discovered an alleged illicit drugs laboratory in Patna, Ayrshire, leading to the arrest of three people.Deputy Chief Constable Jane Connors later described it as the UK's first suspected nitazene laboratory.BBC News can also reveal that two men, aged 43 and 56, were arrested in February this year after police searched a unit in Loanhead, Midlothian, as part of an investigation into another suspected synthetic opioid lab.In 2024, nitazenes were implicated in 76 drug-related deaths in Scotland, according to official figures, external, more than three times the number of the previous year."These drugs are extremely dangerous, and it's pretty rapid for us to be able to keep up as scientists," says Dr Nisbet, whose laboratory is soon set to take on an expanded role as Scotland's national drug testing facility.The changing nature of the supply also creates challenges for lawmakers who are in a race to identify and ban dangerous new substances before they can spread legally and cause havoc."New and harmful substances continue to be created to circumvent legal controls,"  EUDA points out.While control of illicit drugs is reserved to Westminster under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971, responsibility for public health, policing and prosecutions is devolved to the Scottish government and its agencies.Image caption, Gareth Balmer says this is a frightening new landscapeOn the front line of the battle to save lives, charity workers say they are seeing the devastating impact of the new synthetic opioids first-hand.In the woods at Glenbarr on the Kintyre peninsula, staff from the drug, alcohol and mental health charity With You are trying to treat trauma in a group designed to help former drug and alcohol users reconnect with nature.Gareth Balmer, the charity's national harm reduction lead, says nitazenes and other synthetic opioids are now appearing across the drug supply, from benzodiazepine (street Valium) pills and cannabinoids, known as spice, to cocaine and heroin."This is a frightening new landscape," he said. "I don't think drugs have ever been as risky or as dangerous as they are now."The result is that some users are experiencing unexpected and sometimes catastrophic overdoses."Some of these substances are so potent that a grain would be enough to take somebody over," Balmer warned, adding that access to naloxone, which can reverse the effects of an opioid overdose, is now more important than ever.Bull said Police Scotland was taking a twin-track approach, promising to "relentlessly pursue" dealers while also recognising that many drug users need help.In 2025, officers seized about £80m worth of street drugs. So far this year that figure has already reached £78m."Hundreds of individuals have been arrested, and many people are serving custodial sentences," Bull said.But he added that the force also wanted to help users "to make better life choices"."If we come across people who are suffering from addiction, who are in a low point in their life, then we will look to help support them and we'll look to refer them to the relevant agency," he said.Image caption, Prof Niamh Nic Daeid says her team will be able to provide near real-time information to drug-using communitiesProf Niamh Nic Daeid, director of Dundee University's Leverhulme laboratory, said its expanded role as a national drug testing and research centre would make a difference too.On one hand, she said, her team will be able to provide near real-time information to drug-using communities, allowing them to make safer and more informed choices. On the other, the research will help to inform government policy."Drugs are changing all the time," she said. "Part of the establishment of this facility is to have a research capability that will enable us to try to keep up."If we don't know what substances are present in the samples, how can we provide the right advice?"Image caption, Vicky Gamble is worried about the emerging threat of new substancesBack in Kintyre, Vicky Gamble, whose own struggles with alcohol, drugs and crime have seen her in and out of prison, is enjoying the tranquillity of the forest.She is personally hopeful of a better future but she is worried about the emerging threat of new substances and the potential effect on friends and family."It seems that there's a lot of stuff that all the young ones seem to be taking now and I don't even think they know what it is," she told me.For Gareth Balmer of With You, that uncertainty is part of the danger.He says: "It's a terrible thing to say, but with heroin it was better the devil you knew."

schema.headline: The deadly new drugs making Scotland's fight against addiction even harder

title: German elections under way which could decide fate of Chancellor Merz
description: Local elections are taking place in two German states on Sunday which could increase the political pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz.Opinion polls
body: Local elections are taking place in two German states on Sunday which could increase the political pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz.Opinion polls in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommerm suggest Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is at risk of damaging defeats, which would raise further questions about the chancellor's future.These latest elections come after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, while the CDU saw its vote halved.There has been speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced as chancellor mid-term unless the CDU's political fortunes improve.He has said he will carry on but is facing poor approval ratings amid rumours of a so-called chancellor swap, though his challengers are "still hesitating", writes German news site Tagesschau, external.According to the polls, Merz's conservatives could lose power in Berlin as it tussles with Die Linke (The Left) over first place.Meanwhile in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU has only just been hovering above the 5% threshold needed for a party to enter the state parliament. It could spell their worst ever result in a state election.How did it come to this after just 16 months in power? Friedrich Merz is having to answer for the tumbling popularity of his own party, while the political force that he aimed to counter - the AfD - continues its rise.Some branches of the AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects.But its anti-immigration, Russian-friendly, Germany-first agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.The AfD is hoping to build on its recent landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt by topping the polls in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. However, the centre-left SPD has staged a late comeback to be in contention for the top spot through its lead candidate, Manuela Schwesig.Currently the state premier, Schwesig is trying to sweep up the anti-AfD vote as she bills herself as the "Die Frau gegen Blau" - "Woman against Blue", the AfD's party colours.But her local popularity belies the far poorer fortunes of her national party which is locked in a loveless coalition with Merz's CDU.In a queue for a campaign event in the city of Neubrandenburg, AfD supporter Reinhart tells us that the traditional parties are being washed away."Not only in Germany. In Italy, in France, in Great Britain. Everywhere the traditional parties go down."He smiles when asked what he thinks of Merz, saying: "Oh well everyone thinks the same about him."He is arrogant, out of touch, not on the same level as the general public."Merz's backers argue that the chancellor has had a tough time with global events and that a lot of the problems the nation faces are ones he has inherited.But whatever faith people had in his ability to fix those problems, it is apparently ebbing away - and, the brutal truth is, it can be hard to find voters who like him.The former corporate lawyer's tack to the right on issues like immigration has failed to erode AfD support while also alienating people further to the left.His blunt communication style has also caused irritation, such as his dismissal of "work-life balance", telling Germans they need to work more and take less sick leave.Supporters would argue he is a man who is ready to administer the medicine the nation needs, even if people do not like the taste of it.But the country's long-stuttering economy, high energy costs and fraught debates about immigration are feeding a sense of national gloom.Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz and said restoring trust in the CDU lay in "listening ​and taking political action, not in debates ​over personnel".But while no one within his party has openly challenged Merz for the top job, murmurings of discontent have grown louder.Martin Rohloff, the CDU candidate for Neubrandenburg, thinks Merz does not have the "Fingerspitzengefühl, the feeling for the small persons".

schema.headline: German elections under way which could decide fate of Chancellor Merz

title: Eritrea's G-15 political prisoners: 'I don't even know if my parents are alive'
description: Hanna Petros Solomon breaks down in tears as she recalls how she and her siblings effectively became orphans 25 years ago when their father was arrest
body: Hanna Petros Solomon breaks down in tears as she recalls how she and her siblings effectively became orphans 25 years ago when their father was arrested in Eritrea and jailed without trial. Their mother was subsequently detained - and no-one has heard from either of them - or of them - since."He had a towel on his shoulders like a sportsman," she tells the BBC about the last time she saw her father when she was 10 years old, and he had gone out for a jog."He used to work out every morning."Her parents met when they both fought in the long liberation war that saw Eritrea gain independence from Ethiopia in 1993.Her father Petros Solomon had been one of the senior leaders during the war and is regarded by many as a national hero for his critical role.After independence, he had served as defence minister, then foreign minister and had been heading the fisheries ministry when his troubles began.That was in May 2001 when he and 14 other high-profile politicians signed an open letter to President Isaias Afewerki calling for the implementation of a constitution that was ratified after independence and demanding national elections. They became known as the G-15.Isaias, the leader of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF) which had fought against Ethiopia, did not take the criticism well.Unbeknown to Hanna, her father had been dismissed as a minister, though he still went out early to get some exercise each day.It was not until a few days after 9/11 - when the world was distracted by the al-Qaeda attacks on the US - that the country was to discover the full extent of Isaias’s displeasure in what became a watershed moment in Eritrea's history.In the early hours of 18 September, the security forces positioned themselves outside the homes of 11 senior government officials in the capital, Asmara, on the president's orders.Petros was picked up by security agents as he left in his tracksuit.The family had no idea what had happened to him. Hanna and her three siblings went to stay with their paternal grandmother as their mother, Aster Yohannes, was away studying in the US.It was only some days after Petros had disappeared that things became clearer, says Hanna about the painful memories."My classmates told me that my father sold out his country."That is when I understood how serious the situation was, and how people framed my dad and his colleagues who fought for the independence of their country. I was hurt."In the US, Aster was shell-shocked by what had happened - and was in a very bad way. She asked government officials if they could issue the children with passports - but they refused, telling her to come home.After agonising about the situation for two years and reportedly receiving assurances from government officials, she packed her bags to return.Hanna and her siblings desperately wanted her back - but they were also worried."I told her on the phone: 'What if they arrest you?'" Hanna remembers."She insisted nothing would happen to her, saying: 'I haven't done anything wrong, and am only coming to raise my children.'"Hanna says she learned later that President Isaias himself had promised Aster that she would be safe. But while the family waited at Asmara International Airport on 11 December 2003, she failed to emerge through arrivals with the other passengers.Their hopes began to wilt along with the flowers they had brought: "It was a long, long wait. Eventually we gave up and went back home."First we called to the US, friends and relatives told us they saw her off at the airport."Then ominously an official called from the airport asking Aster to collect her luggage. That is when they realised she had arrived in the country but would not be coming home.All pleas and requests for information fell on deaf ears in the months that followed. Instead Hanna's grandmother was warned by authorities to stop inquiring.The family later heard that Aster was being held in the infamous jail known as Karshelli in the heart of Asmara.Hanna's father is believed to be detained, with the others arrested on 18 and 19 September 2001, in the remote, hostile and highly secretive prison known as Ela-Ero, located in eastern lowlands north-east of Asmara. Accused of treason, none of them has ever been brought to trial or allowed to see their relatives.At around the same time, the government also shut down all the fledgling independent newspapers and detained their editors and journalists - also believed to be imprisoned in Ela-Ero.The Eritrean government - including its embassy in the UK - has not responded to the BBC's request for comment regarding the whereabouts of the prisoners or whether or not they are alive.Hanna, like many thousands of young Eritreans fleeing conscription and in search of better opportunities, left the country - travelling secretively over the border without a passport.Now 35 years old, she is married and lives in the US, working as a trauma specialist - but still feels traumatised herself by how she lost her parents.As she stares at old pictures of her parents, she worries her memories will fade of the happy times before their arrest - the laughter, the family gatherings, the birthday parties: "My dad always wanted to gather people in the house, they were good days."She also hankers after her mother's "unmatched" egg and potato sandwiches.On trips down to the coast when her father was the minister of fisheries, Hanna remembers him organising singing competitions in the car: "He would ask us to sing one by one and whoever won would get a present."One of his favourite songs included the lyrics: "I had a sweater, a blue sweater, that my sister took" - which reminded him of his sister who was also a freedom fighter and had been killed during the war.She also has memories of her mother loving music - playing and singing hits by Abba, Dolly Parton and Whitney Houston.Until her father's arrest, Hanna remembers September as being full of hope with its three big Orthodox Christian festivals, including the Geez New Year. Now the month brings her no joy.Ibrahim Sherifo knows exactly how she feels. Both his parents, who were senior members of the ruling People's Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ), were among the G-15 people arrested 25 years ago.He was 13 years old at the time"For me 18 September 2001 is a dark day, but not only for me, it is a dark day for Eritrea and its people, because it is the day when law and democracy was detained," he tells the BBC. He is now 38 and living in exile in the Netherlands, where he was granted asylum, and is pursuing an MA in political science - following in his father's footsteps.His dad Mahmoud Ahmed Sherifo was the local government minister and de facto deputy president before his detention.Ibrahim was with his mother, Aster Fissehatsion, staying with her sister when he remembers security agents knocking on the door early in the morning and taking her away in her pyjamas.Worried about his father, Ibrahim immediately ran to his nearby house but was told he had already been picked up when he had gone out for exercise.Both Hanna and Ibrahim say they are forever grateful to the friends and family who offered them care and supported them as they grew up without their parents, despite the risks.They are also proud of what their parents stood for and daring to call for reforms."They had conscience and couldn't observe idly while what they fought for what had been hijacked by Isaias and his coterie," says Ibrahim."As a family, we should be informed whether they are alive or not," he adds, accusing the government of wanting to erase all memory of the political prisoners.Hanna also wants the plight of the many others whose relatives have disappeared over the years to be heard too.Human rights groups, including the UN, consider the G-15 prisoners of conscience and have been calling for their release.President Isaias, now 80, has still not implemented the country's first constitution - approved in 1997 - and remains in power without ever holding an election.Hanna recalls that on the eve of her father's disappearance, she had a "bad feeling" - and had crept into his bed and tied his legs to her own with string while he slept."In the morning he woke up to find he was tied up and to release himself he pulled my legs and I woke up. I begged him not to leave but he assured me that he would return [after his run]."Describing the years of sorrow since, she says it is like living in the deep sea."Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down."Sometimes you lose hope and you are out of breath."Asked what she would say if she could get a message to her parents, she replies: "Don't worry about us."Like you survived the struggle through sheer steadfastness, we hope you can pull through this too and return to us."

schema.headline: Eritrea's G-15 political prisoners: 'I don't even know if my parents are alive'

title: Meta glasses: Is it okay to film people in public places?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Meta said it recently updated the glasses to disable the camera if the light was tampered withByOlivia Copela
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Meta said it recently updated the glasses to disable the camera if the light was tampered withByOlivia CopelandBBC News NIIt's the latest wearable tech boom that is likely coming to a street, park or town square near you. But not everyone sees the future of smart glasses as rose-tinted.The technology allows users to make calls, interact with AI hands-free and also take photos and videos simply by touching the frames, provoking concerns about privacy.Wetherspoons, which runs almost 800 pubs across the UK, has banned using the glasses to film inside its premises and women's rights campaigners have raised issues about their potential use for harassment.But, with videos from content creators continuing to thrive on social media platforms like TikTok and Instagram, the debate of how to best use the glasses in public places will continue to go back and forth.Pearse Vallely is one of those content creators – the 31-year-old from Ballymurphy, in west Belfast, makes a living from his work on social media.He uses a pair of Meta Ray-Ban glasses, with most of his videos showing his glasses-eye view of walking down the street as he greets passers-by with rhyming phrases.One of his most popular videos, filmed in Belfast city centre, hit 600,000 views on TikTok.Image source, Pearse VallelyImage caption, Content creator Pearse Vallely, wearing his Meta glasses, said he uses them "in a positive way"The success of the videos rely on their good-natured vibe. He said he had never posted a video after being asked not to, and no one had ever got in touch to ask him to take down a video."I think it's because of the nature of my conversation with them. They know I'm not making an eejit out of them, I'm doing it in a positive way."Meta glasses, the brand used by Vallely, are the market leader in the smart glasses boom, with the company saying more than seven million pairs have been sold to date.This TikTok post cannot be displayed in your browser. Please enable Javascript or try a different browser.View original content on TikTokThe BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites. TikTok content may contain adverts.Skip tiktok video by Pearsey-WearseyAllow TikTok content?This article contains content provided by TikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. You may want to read TikTok’s cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’.The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites. TikTok content may contain adverts.Available for a few hundred pounds, and made in partnership with the firm behind famed sunglasses brand Ray-Bans, the frames feature an unobtrusive camera that users can activate via touch.This turns on a pulsing white light, which aims to let people know when a video is being taken, and a flash for photos – a feature a Meta spokesperson said "smartphones and other cameras don't have".Meta said it recently updated the glasses to disable the camera if the light was tampered with.Should AI or smart glasses products from more companies end up selling as well as Meta's version, researchers expect as many as 100 million people will buy a pair in the next few years.Valelly, whose videos rely on the interactions being spontaneous and natural, said people are often aware he is recording due to the light on his glasses.He also said he tries to let people know he has recorded them after filming if he can catch them in time.In Northern Ireland, it is generally legal to film someone even discreetly in a public place, as people in public do not usually have a reasonable expectation of privacy.The filming would only be unlawful if it could be seen as harassment, stalking, if the footage is voyeuristic, or in circumstances where there would be a reasonable expectation of privacy.Image caption, The smart glasses can be used to make calls hands-free, play music in ear and take photos and videos"It's okay to have a 30-second conversation with someone," Vallely said."I think that's something we're losing due to technology, and I'm trying to use technology to spin it around."Vallely said he could understand the reasoning behind banning wearing Meta glasses "if people are being crude and rude", but he said the intention behind filming was key."People know it's me doing it, while other people do it on troll accounts. No matter what is invented, people are going to use things for the wrong reasons."Still, while Vallely said he hasn't run into any opposition, there are reports suggesting an increased friction between people using the glasses to film and the general public.Last December, people hailed a woman as "a hero" after she snapped a man's Meta glasses in two on the New York subway. In July, police in Scotland began an investigation after complaints over a TikToker who used the glasses to secret film members of the public.Referring to the company's ban on filming, a Wetherspoons spokesperson said smart glasses breached "common sense by enabling surreptitious surveillance" while Monopoly Events, which runs Comic Con Northern Ireland, also banned wearing the glasses at its events over concerns about secret recording.Meanwhile, TikTok videos of users approaching women, asking for their number and filming their reaction to pick-up lines, are often posted with the hashtag #howtogetagirlfriend and can garner thousands of views.Harassment concernsImage caption, Women's rights campaigners say the glasses pose risks to privacyElaine Crory, a women's sector lobbyist at the Women's Resource and Development Agency, said there's a lack of awareness about when and how the glasses are being used, leading to issues around consent."Right now, if you're filming with a camera or with your phone, I usually can see that and then avoid that. But you may not be aware you're being filmed with an AI camera."She added there were also concerns the glasses were being used for things that are currently illegal, like upskirting.Crory said people can appeal to social media sites to take videos down and some venues have put up signs "on a case by case basis", but she feels legislation has not caught up with the technology."A person has no legal redress if they are filmed in the street, on a bus, in a classroom," she said.The Department of Justice (DoJ) said that while the regulation of Meta glasses was not a DoJ specific matter, if the use of the glasses involved "behaviour that crosses the criminal threshold, then existing offences such as 'up-skirting' as a form of voyeurism" were available.Image caption, Optometrist Geoff McConville says the glasses are "ground-breaking" for visually-impaired usersFor optometrist Geoff McConville, who stocks Meta glasses in his Belfast shop, there are concerns about their "inappropriate use", but there are also beneficial aspects to the technology.He cites how his patients use text-to-speech features, allowing them to read newspapers and signs with AI."For my elderly, visually impaired patients, they are ground-breaking. They are amazing."In a statement, Meta said the glasses provided "critical new technology for people who are low-sighted or hard of hearing and limiting how people can use this technology would be a major step backwards"."Naturally some places shouldn't be filmed at all and that's reasonable but rules should be applied consistently."In a recent Q&A session, the head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, said if people posted content "taking advantage of people and harassing them... then we're going to take the content down".

schema.headline: Meta glasses: Is it okay to film people in public places?

title: Our head teacher was an abuser. We joined forces to get justice - now we're married
description: The full story with be available in subsequent episodes of World of Secrets Catching My TeacherWatch the full investigation on iPlayer from 0001 Monda
body: The full story with be available in subsequent episodes of World of Secrets Catching My TeacherWatch the full investigation on iPlayer from 0001 Monday 21 September. If you are outside the UK, you will be able watch on YouTubeYusron began investigating Abah a year previously, sparked by a revelation one night by his former classmate Ziadatur Rahmah. They had both been star pupils at Lombok's Abu Barokat school. Now they were at university - Yusron in the capital Jakarta, and Ziadatur in Cairo, Egypt - and had begun reminiscing over the phone about their school days.One night Ziadatur, known to her friends as Zia, told Yusron that Abah had sexually assaulted her when she was 16.She had needed to go to the toilet during class and Abah had intercepted her in the school gardens and asked her to accompany him to his house which was on the premises. Once inside, he had told her he loved her, she told Yusron."He pulled me down so I was sitting on his lap… Then he started kissing me… He was stroking and touching my body," she later told the BBC World Service, too, explaining that he told her to do the same to him.Luckily, she said, one of his children began banging on the locked front door. Abah signalled to her to leave and she bolted out the back. But the effect was devastating."I felt very dirty, ruined, and I was lost."Yusron, when he heard Zia's account, was unsure what to do. Their school had inculcated them with the motto: "Sami'na wa ata'na" ["We hear, and we obey"].But he also could not stop thinking about it.So he suggested that he and Zia, together with her school friends Wanda Hamidah and Mahima Eka, gather corroborating evidence to support her testimony.And slowly, as they spoke to their old classmates, other recollections emerged - the friends sharing their findings with each other on WhatsApp.The most significant was from a friend of Wanda's. She recalled seeing a younger girl crying in the school bathroom during their final year, late at night. And that Abah had come looking for her, red-faced and panting.This girl, Sukma Rohana, was still at the school. She told the BBC about her ordeal.When Sukma was 17, Abah had asked her to join him for new year's prayers, she told us. When she entered Abah's house, he had covered her mouth and told her to lie down, she said, before he stripped below the waist."He kept talking, saying he couldn't control himself any more," Sukma said."He was feeling me up through my knickers… He tried to rape me."And then, she said, she had found the strength to kick him hard in the stomach and took the opportunity to flee.As she ran, she said she had looked back to see his torch seeking her out.As evidence like this emerged, Yusron would co-ordinate it - following up with calls to the students making the allegations, and keeping painstaking notes.He typed up a seven-page document outlining the alleged abuse of Sukma, Zia and four other former students.Wanda organised a meeting with representatives from the Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI) - the powerful organisation that ran their school and hundreds of others, and which was also funding some of the students' studies in Cairo.The meeting went well, the friends told us - the NWDI representatives had said they would help them take the case to the police.But three weeks later, when Yusron received that ominous text from his sister - calling back to find Abah on the end of the phone in Yusron's family home - it became clear the NWDI had passed on Yusron's written documents to him."If this is leaked to the media… I'll be destroyed," Abah can be heard saying on Yusron's recording of him.He pleads with Yusron to lie for him, giving him a series of cover stories he can use to retract his evidence document.He then called Zia and exerted similar pressure. Like Yusron, she recorded the call. In it, Abah admits he abused her but pleads with her to stay silent.Sukma, for her part, told us she was called to Abah's house to discover two police officers and an NWDI lawyer waiting for her. They forced her to sign a document saying all her allegations were lies, she said. Her account is backed up by a secret recording she later made as she challenged Abah's wife, Hurmiati.Hurmiati can be heard telling her to respect their "agreement" that nothing happened, adding: "Do you want this to haunt you for the rest of your life? Do you want it to damage the chances of you getting married?"This pressure even extended to Abah asking Yusron's parents to fly to Jakarta to look for him at university. They didn't find him - he was hiding in a hotel - but the ordeal was too much for Yusron's mother. She told her son the stress was killing her.So Yusron reluctantly stopped his investigation.Meanwhile he and Zia were slowly getting closer. The friendship had become a long-distance relationship, and they were regularly speaking on the phone."And I could see she was really struggling… She'd say things like: 'Why do I keep thinking about what [Abah] did?'."Yusron was torn between helping the girl he was falling in love with, and the promise he had made to his mother.And then, eight months later, Yusron heard about a group raising awareness about sexual abuse in Islamic schools. It had been set up by a young woman called Ayu Masruroh, who had helped her friend get justice after she had been sexually assaulted at another school, by a teacher called Moch Subchi Azal Tsani.Ayu was now actively posting on social media about the need to speak out.It inspired Zia to post a call-out on Instagram, asking any Indonesian student who had experienced abuse to get in touch.And she was to discover that, despite Abah's remonstrations, and promises to change, he had apparently offended again. Someone who went to Zia's school got in touch to say she too had been sexually exploited by Abah. The alleged abuse had taken place almost a year after his pledges to Zia and Yusron."It made me realise [Abah] hadn't really changed at all… all the things he said about stopping… It was all just lies," said Zia.If you are in the UK, and have been affected by issues of sexual abuse or violence, information and support is available at BBC Action LineYusron's parents finally agreed he should help Zia and Sukma to continue their quest for justice.But this time, the friends decided to do things differently. They contacted Ayu, and she was clear: get a lawyer. She introduced them to someone experienced in representing sexual abuse survivors. He advised that Sukma's case was the strongest to ensure a prosecution.We contacted Abah and Hurmiati about the allegations against them - they did not respond.NWDI said it was still investigating the allegations internally and denied ever trying to cover up sexual abuse claims.It said it had "a duty to safeguard the organisation from being tarnished by the alleged actions of individuals".Sukma filed her claim against Abah to the police in February last year. She is still waiting for them to take action and Abah is still in post."I don't want what happened to me, to happen to any other students. I want justice," she told the BBC.The investigation has, however, brought Zia and Yusron ever closer. Last February, after three years of messaging and speaking, Yusron decided to move to Cairo to be with her."I was exhausted. Jakarta had been intense, because I was dealing with the police case the whole time. So when I saw Zia… it was like medicine," he told the BBC.Zia said she was so happy she "started talking non-stop."That's when I knew he was serious. He had come all the way to Egypt for me. I trust him. That's why I'm with him."It is a trust built, in part, on their shared pursuit of justice. Last month the couple got married.Their lawyer, Joko Jumadi, says he has been struck by the students' courage and precision.The recordings they secretly collected, he told us, capture the pressure to stay silent in real time and are exceptionally valuable. "Several victims are mentioned - acknowledged by the individual himself. These are key pieces of evidence," he said.Joko and his team have handled 20 sexual abuse cases involving Islamic boarding schools in his local West Nusa Tenggara province over the past three years, and he believes this is "just the tip of the iceberg".

schema.headline: Our head teacher was an abuser. We joined forces to get justice - now we're married

title: Twin's stillbirth inspires grieving Stratford father's children's book
description: Warning: This story covers stillbirths and some people may find the details distressingOne date is etched into Richard Ganjavi's memory: 6 August 2024
body: Warning: This story covers stillbirths and some people may find the details distressingOne date is etched into Richard Ganjavi's memory: 6 August 2024. It was the day for the routine 34-week scan for the twins he was expecting with his wife, Naomi."The room went quiet. [The woman doing the scan] said the words that shattered everything: "I'm so sorry, there isn't a heartbeat."Naomi and Richard were rushed from Stratford Hospital to Warwick Hospital but Bella was stillborn."We just fell to pieces," Richard said.In the time since then, Bella's twin sister, Penny, who was born healthily, has just celebrated her second birthday. In those two years, Richard said he processed his grief by writing a children's book, Whispers of a Purple Butterfly, inspired by his story.The primary school teacher started writing within weeks of the loss of Bella."We had two cots upstairs, two seats in the car, a double pram. Two years on we could be walking down the street, and see someone with twins and every time it just gets you," he admitted."In a way you never get over it."The book is about Lucy, a fictional 10-year-old who is the surviving twin of a similar situation and aimed at eight to 12 year olds.Richard, who lives in Meon Vale, near Stratford-upon-Avon, said the process was "a way of getting it down and out of my head".But  the novel has since taken on a larger meaning for the family with Richard reading it to Penny, so she has something when she is old enough to understand, "to know that she will always be enough".The reaction from those who have read the book had blown Richard away, he admitted."I've had so many messages from bereaved parents, people who've lost a family member or a close friend," he said."They've all said, after reading the book, 'wow, where was it when I needed it'."He hoped charities, teachers and therapists could use the book to help those dealing with the loss of a baby.Richard and Naomi make regular visits to the hospital's Rainbow Garden, where Bella has a glass leaf in her memory.They have become friends with nurses and midwives at the special care baby unit who looked after Penny as well as them, after the loss of Bella.Two of the midwives went on to become Penny's godmothers."We've really built a relationship with Richard and Naomi, and it's really lovely to see them coming back," Lead nurse Bettina Powell said."It's really important...to remember the loss of Bella.""It's been so lovely watching Penny grow, seeing how they navigate everything and all the things they've done," neonatal nurse Teri added."It's been so lovely feeling part of their journey."Richard said he wanted his book be become a lasting legacy for Bella"We are so proud of Penny but we're also proud of Bella. When we talk about her, we say her name with pride," he said."The grief doesn't go away, but the world around our grief has got bigger."If you have been affected by the issues raised in this story, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Twin's stillbirth inspires grieving Stratford father's children's book

title: Folkestone council evacuates nearby residents after Grand Burstin hotel fire
description: A council spokesperson said that Pavilion Court residents had been given hotel accommodation in the town, adding that it was "working to arrange alter
body: A council spokesperson said that Pavilion Court residents had been given hotel accommodation in the town, adding that it was "working to arrange alternative housing for all affected residents while the Grand Burstin undergoes further assessments and any required works to make it safe".In a statement, Britannia Hotels Group, which runs the Grand Burstin, said that it was fully cooperating with Kent Police and supporting the investigation into the circumstances surrounding the fire.The group thanked emergency service personnel, adding: "Engineers and building inspectors are now on site conducting structural assessments and our team is working hard to assist all guests with their immediate needs. "We remain in close contact with all relevant authorities and we appreciate everyone's patience and understanding during this developing situation."A total of 26 fire engines were sent to the hotel at about 01:05 BST on Saturday, Kent Fire & Rescue Service said, adding: "It's believed the fire started in the basement of the property."On Sunday, a fire service spokesperson said that the firefighting operation had ended, and the scene had been handed over to Kent Police.Station manager Lawrence Pater said that the "very severe" fire had raised concerns about the structural integrity of the building and that the fire service was seeking advice from inspectors.Folkestone & Hythe District Council set up a welfare centre at the Three Hills Sports Park for hotel residents evacuated on Saturday.Other local businesses, including nearby pub The Harbour Inn, also opened their doors to those affected.Speaking to the BBC, John Dighton, who was evacuated from Pavilion Court, said that he was told to leave his flat at about 19:00 on Saturday.The 50-year-old said: "We don't know how long we will be out for but we have grabbed stuff for a couple of days."The worst thing is the not knowing. We are at a hotel over the road from the flats."Ross Honeycomb, 39, was staying at the hotel with his family and told the BBC on Saturday how they were woken by fire alarms at about 01:00.He said: "I thought I was dreaming, it was horrifying."We looked out and there was smoke billowing from the underground car park. Later we started hearing explosions."Kevin Crawford, 91, and his wife Kathleen, 82, said they had booked in for a two-week stay at the hotel.The couple, from London, told the BBC that they were in their room on the sixth floor when they heard a fire alarm."We saw the fire but we thought the fire brigade had it under control," said Kevin."We managed to sleep through it. At the time, we didn't realise how bad the fire was."The council's chief executive, Susan Priest, said on Saturday: "The extent of support of organisations, including Three Hills, Morrisons and the Salvation Army, has been amazing and helped to ensure that visitors and residents were looked after, supported and had food and hot drinks."This was an extremely difficult day, firstly for the hotel guests and this evening for our residents who have had to move out of their homes."

schema.headline: Folkestone council evacuates nearby residents after Grand Burstin hotel fire

title: Oldham Asian hornet hunt leads to nest discovery
description: Image source, HandoutImage caption, Food traps were used to attract the hornets before monitoring the direction and timing of their flightsByMichelle
body: Image source, HandoutImage caption, Food traps were used to attract the hornets before monitoring the direction and timing of their flightsByMichelle AdamsonReporting fromin Oldham and Naj ModakNorth WestBeekeepers who feared a damaging new arrival of Asian hornets in the Greater Manchester area helped track down their nest after sightings sparked an urgent search.The nest of the non-native invasive insects, which prey on honey bees and threaten biodiversity, was found in Oldham, after local keepers worked with government bee inspectors to trace them using GPS trackers and food traps.The Asian hornets were first spotted three weeks ago in Oldham, prompting concerns the species may be spreading further north.Beekeeper, Cath Charnock, said: "We weren't expecting to see any this soon in our area."Image caption, Local beekeepers Cath Charnock and Les Latham worked alongside government bee inspectors to trace the insectsCharnock said two credible sightings were received within a short period, which prompted them to take action.Fellow beekeeper Les Latham said the team used food traps to attract the insects before monitoring the direction and timing of their flights.By repeating the process at different locations, they were able to build up a picture of where the nest was likely to be.Government bee inspectors then joined the search, using GPS radio trackers and AI-assisted cameras to narrow down the location.Image source, HandoutImage caption, A single nest could consume about 15kg (two stone) of insects in one seasonLatham said several search teams eventually converged on the same spot before inspectors used binoculars to identify the nest in a tree.A single nest could consume about 15kg (two stone) of insects in one season, affecting not only honeybees but also hoverflies, moths, spiders, wasps and other species, she said.Charnock urged the public to report suspected sightings using the Asian Hornet Watch app, calling on people to "see it, snap it and app it".Asian hornets pose no greater threat to humans than native hornets, and if you get stung by one, the advice is to immediately wash the area with cold water and soap, then apply ice to stop the venom spreading further.But the main prey of the Asian hornet is honeybees, with one insect killing up to 50 bees a day, devastating entire colonies.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Greater Manchester

schema.headline: Oldham Asian hornet hunt leads to nest discovery

title: Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King
description: ByAndré Rhoden-Paul Earl Spencer has told the BBC writing his book about sister Princess Diana, which has made headlines for its criticism of King Cha
body: ByAndré Rhoden-Paul Earl Spencer has told the BBC writing his book about sister Princess Diana, which has made headlines for its criticism of King Charles, was his "duty...as an eyewitness to history".In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the memoir's release on Tuesday, Earl Spencer said he wanted "to put things down once and for all that were true".Among claims made in Swan Song: Diana, My Sister about the King, who was then the Prince of Wales, was that he said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".Here are the key moments from Earl Spencer's interview, which include his first account of how he was told about Diana's death and criticism of press coverage of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex. Earl initially told Diana crash was 'not too serious'Earl Spencer was in South Africa when Princess Diana died in a Paris car crash in the early hours of 31 August 1997, along with close friend Dodi Fayed and the driver of the car.He told the BBC he got a call in the middle of the night from his sister Lady Jane Fellowes, who said Princess Diana had been in a crash but "it's not too serious". But then he "kept getting more and more distressing calls" from his sister. "And then my sister Jane said, 'I'm afraid she's died.' It started... as a little prang, and then it became a broken leg, perhaps a head injury, and then death."Charles had 'giddy tone' after Diana's deathDescribing the hours after her death, Earl Spencer said he took a call at his home in Cape Town from Prince Charles, who told him how he broke the news to Princes William and Harry at Balmoral Castle. "I felt there was a sort of giddy tone," he told the BBC. "I'd had a lot of calls that day from people who cared, who were stunned... and I just felt there was a lightness in his tone about Diana's death that really jarred with me."In his book, Earl Spencer compares his tone to like a "lottery winner" and says he suspects the prince's reaction was based on how this event would free him to marry the woman he loved, his future wife Queen Camilla. When asked by Kuenssberg if he could be sure that is what Prince Charles was thinking, Earl Spencer said: "I cannot be sure, I'm saying that's what I assume from the tone is a possibility." Image caption, Princess Diana: My Sister's Story. The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg is available on BBC iPlayer and will be broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday Earl Spencer told the BBC he had been discussing funeral arrangements with a palace official, who said it had been agreed Princes William and Harry should walk behind their mother's coffin. Unhappy, he said he told the official it is not what his sister would have wanted, before the conversation came to an end. Soon after, the earl says he took a call from Prince Charles, who asked him about his opposition to it. "I said, 'Well, of course not, sir, she wouldn't want it'. And then he said, 'Well, I walked behind Lord Mountbatten's coffin.' And I said, 'Yes, but you were 30 and he wasn't your mother'."He then claims Charles went "ballistic... and ranted for a while" about the Spencer's sense of duty not being adequate enough before "he said 'We'll forget her [Diana] soon enough'.""I really was so stunned and after a stunned silence I said 'I can not believe you just said that' and I hung up on him", the earl told Kuenssberg during his sit down interview at his Althorp estate. Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Princes William and Harry walked in the procession behind their mother's coffinResponding to the Palace's statement pushing back on the story, Earl Spencer said: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said. "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage in my life. "I was hyper-alert to what he was saying, and those are precisely the words he said. And I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. "I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."The earl said he told "close friends and family" about the "monstrous" comment. When asked if people should believe him or the King, he said: "Well, I'm telling the truth... what else would have made me hang up on the King that day?"On what Princes William and Harry might think of the comments being brought up nearly 30 years later, he added the words "will not be a surprise" to the brothers.He also said his renowned funeral eulogy, in which he said his sister's qualities would never be "extinguished from our minds", was a "direct rebuttal" of the prince's comments. 'I know lots of things about the King' not in the bookTalking about his motivations for writing the book, Earl Spencer, aged 62, said it was his "duty... as an eyewitness to history" and as someone in the "final season of my life" with his parents dying in their sixties."I'm aware of mortality and I wanted to just put things down once and for all that were true," the historian and journalist explained."This is not a threat, it's a fact, I know lots of things about the King which I chose not to include in the book because they were not relevant."When put to him that the  statement sounded like a threat when it involved potentially damaging information, he said: "No, not at all a threat, it's just the reality."Kuenssberg questioned why he included an account of a conversation in which his sister told him Prince Charles was in love with his valet - a claim Earl Spencer said was improbable - and asked if he was motivated in including some of these allegations to create interest to sell the book. "It's in the context of a conversation where Diana is telling me that her marriage is over," the earl replied."It's a brother's tribute, a loving tribute to a sister.  And I think she deserves honesty so that's what I've delivered."The earl said he considers Swan Song to be his "sign off" and final take on the situation. "I'm not here to bang on about Diana, this is my final word, celebration of her, and I will step off into the sunset now and not be available for comment."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Earl Spencer said he was concerned about security for Duke and Duchess of SussexWhen asked about how he thinks Prince Harry has been treated by the Royal Family,   Earl Spencer tells the BBC he is reluctant to discuss it, but he said he was concerned about his security. "I would say that I personally worry about the fifth-in-line to the throne who's served in the military not having any police protection," he said. "As an uncle who's seen his sister die in very, very preventable circumstances, that I would veer towards protection."It is understood the committee that oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now they and their two children are full-time residents in the UK rather than visitors.When asked about how the press treated Princess Diana and now Prince Harry and Meghan, he said tabloid articles "could be really really unpleasant". "It would really be beholden on people to learn from Diana's example. I'm not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who's being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life," Earl Spencer said. "[Diana] was really brought low by all that criticism. And yeah I suppose it's a pity when I see echoes of that now."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The earl said he hopes his nephews resolve their differences'I hope William and Harry resolve row' Earl Spencer said he did not take sides - as he perceives is the "perception in the media" - in the dispute between Princes William and Harry. "I'm on my deceased sister's sons' side, both of them. And if either of them wanted anything then I'd be equally there for them," he said. "And I never get involved in one camp or the other, except as a benign figure I hope."He said there are a "lot of reasons on both sides" why the brothers' relationship had "got to this stage". "I hope one day it's resolved, but I don't know all – I certainly don't know what's been done in the finer detail and so I would feel intrusive if I got more involved than to say of course a mother would want her two sons to be happy together and love each other," he said. Diana 'convinced she couldn't trust people' after Bashir interviewReflecting on the time before Princess Diana's death, Kuenssberg asked if the infamous BBC Panorama interview with journalist Martin Bashir in 1995 might have been linked indirectly to his sister finding herself in Paris in 1997. Shortly after the interview broadcast, in which Princess Diana admitted having an affair and said Prince Charles's affair with then-Camilla Parker Bowles made her feel worthless, the Queen wrote to Prince Charles and Princess Diana telling them to divorce.A 2021 inquiry found Bashir acted in a "deceitful" way  by mocking up fake bank statements - which falsely suggested individuals were being paid to keep Diana under surveillance - and showing them to Earl Spencer to gain access to the late princess.Earl Spencer said he did make "a connection" between the crash and the Panorama interview and said they conned both him and Diana."People said, 'Oh, she was paranoid,'. She wasn't paranoid. She was convinced that she couldn't trust people because the evidence was there.  And, you know, I think that left her vulnerable that night."The BBC and Bashir apologised to King Charles, Earl Spencer and Princes William and Harry after the 2021 report was published.The BBC's then-director general, Tim Davie, said: "Although the report states that Diana, Princess of Wales, was keen on the idea of an interview with the BBC, it is clear that the process for securing the interview fell far short of what audiences have a right to expect. We are very sorry for this."Earl supports 'a modern monarchy'Earl Spencer, the ninth earl of an aristocratic family whose peerage dates back to the 18th Century and retains its vast estate, told the BBC he is "all for a monarchy, but I like a modern monarchy". Talking about the "jarring" protocol around the monarchy, he said: "You know, you mentioned the statement earlier, 'His Majesty says", I just don't think it's healthy for a human being to be seen in such archaic, servile terms."When Kuenssberg asked him if he supported this monarchy, following the damning book he has just written, he said: "I do."He added when challenged: "Well, I'm not dealing with King Charles as monarch in this book, this is all 30-odd years ago and what was said and done then."

schema.headline: Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King

title: Charles said Diana would be forgotten 'soon enough', Earl Spencer claims in book
description: Buckingham Palace has responded after a claim by Earl Spencer, the brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, that King Charles said "we'll forget her soon
body: Buckingham Palace has responded after a claim by Earl Spencer, the brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, that King Charles said "we'll forget her soon enough" days after her death.Earl Spencer alleged the then-Prince of Wales subjected him to a "stream of anger" after he insisted Diana would not have wanted Princes William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, to walk in her funeral procession.The claim was made in an extract from his upcoming memoir, published by the Daily Mail.A Palace spokesperson said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family. BBC News has not seen the book in full.In the first extract, external from it to be made public, Earl Spencer claims to have been informed by a senior Palace aide that the young princes would walk alongside Princess Diana's coffin, which he objected to.He claims to have received a phone call from Charles shortly after.Earl Spencer wrote in the book: "He [Charles] unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough'."Earl Spencer's book about his sister seems set to open a very difficult time in the recent history of the Royal Family.The death of Diana, a hugely popular figure, in a car crash in 1997, had created a volatile atmosphere, in which the royals were accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and had seemed out of touch with the public mood.Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Diana's untimely death.Prince Harry has previously said that walking behind his mother's coffin aged 12 was something no child "should be asked to do". In 2017, he told the BBC he didn't "have an opinion whether that was right or wrong", but "looking back on it", he was glad to have been part of the day.Earlier on Wednesday, it emerged that copies of Earl Spencer's unreleased book had been stolen from a truck in the Netherlands.BBC News understands four copies of the Dutch language edition were taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher's printers to their warehouse.

title: Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses moral high ground by living in tax exile - Labour Party Chair
description: The Labour Party chair has said Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses "the moral high ground" by making statements about the UK while living in tax exile.Speaking t
body: The Labour Party chair has said Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses "the moral high ground" by making statements about the UK while living in tax exile.Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Bridget Phillipson said she would take the billionaire businessman's comments that the UK was "on the slide" with a "pinch of salt".Sir Jim, the founder of petrochemical giant Ineos and Manchester United's co-owner, told the BBC he has lost confidence in the UK due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.He has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020 and said "things would have to get better" in the UK for him to return.When questioned over the remarks, Phillipson said Sir Jim loses "the moral high ground" by "making these kinds of pronouncements while choosing to make decisions, that he is within his rights to make, to become a tax exile".Pushed on whether it bothers her that people who create jobs and pay a lot of tax were leaving the UK, the minister said she was "optimistic about our country's prospects".Other high profile billionaires have left the UK, including including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently the UK's third biggest taxpayer, hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos.But, Philipson argued the country was in a good position ahead of the Budget next month, and Andy Burnham has shown a "sense of hope and optimism whilst recognising that many families are still struggling and there is more to do.""Of course, there are challenges, including big international headwinds, but I fundamentally believe that we are in a strong position going into this budget because of the decisions taken over the last two years, and I believe our country's best days lie ahead of us," she said.Philipson declined to speculate over whether there would be tax rises in the Budget on 28 October, and said the government remained committed to being disciplined about its spending rules.

schema.headline: Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses moral high ground by living in tax exile - Labour Party Chair
